Executive Summary

Your 86.9 kW SolarEdge system produced 104,934 kWh during the analysis period, representing a specific yield of 1,207 kWh/kWp — production consistent with expected performance for this site.

Your exported solar energy is being credited consistently with the expected operation of Net Energy Metering 2.0. We validated your exports against SCE's interval data and found no discrepancy.

Approximately 82% of your modeled variable electric cost comes from demand charges — a fee based on your single highest 15-minute power draw each month, not total energy used. This is a demand-dominant account: demand, not energy consumption, is the primary driver of your bill. Your relatively low energy charge reflects your solar system operating as expected, offsetting most of your energy usage.

Primary Cost Drivers

Your modeled annual cost at current rates is $19,976, composed of:

  • Facilities demand charge — $12,906 (65%): a fee based on your single highest 15-minute power draw each month.
  • Time-related demand charge — $3,549 (18%): a second demand fee tied to when that peak occurs.
  • Energy charge — $3,520 (18%): the electricity you actually use, priced by time of day.

Note: your energy charge is low relative to demand charges because your solar asset already offsets most of your energy use — see Solar Asset Production Value below.

Your annual peak demand reached 43.2 kW. Your building carries a steady ~7.8 kW overnight baseload — a practical opportunity for future operational savings.

Recommendations

SCE Rate Optimization

We recommend changing your rate schedule from TOU-GS-2-D to TOU-GS-2-E, together with monthly performance monitoring.

Current Plan

TOU-GS-2-D
Modeled annual cost: $19,976

Recommended Plan

TOU-GS-2-E
Modeled annual cost: $12,396

Estimated annual savings: $5,000–$7,000.

Why This Works

TOU-GS-2-D is demand-weighted; TOU-GS-2-E is energy-weighted. Because your solar already offsets a meaningful share of your energy use, shifting toward energy pricing lowers your total projected cost — same facility, same equipment.

Operating Profile

Your building draws a steady ~7.8 kW overnight, every night — it never fully powers down. Grid draw climbs to ~14 kW around 8:00 AM, just before solar ramps up. After hours (6 PM–7 AM), average draw of 7.5 kW exceeds your solar-masked midday load.

Battery Storage Assessment

Your demand peaks occur at 8:30–9:00 AM, just before solar ramps up — a window solar can't reach, but a battery could. If a battery fully offset your morning peak (roughly 5–8 kW), demand-charge savings could plausibly fall in the range of $1,500–$3,000/year — a hypothetical estimate, not a modeled figure.

Turning this into a firm recommendation requires 15-minute interval production data from SCE (not just daily SolarEdge totals) to isolate how much of the morning peak is real building load versus solar still ramping up, and to size a battery correctly.

Billing Corrections Audit (2022–2023)

Finding

Historical correction bills (6 PDFs issued Oct 9, 2023) re-issue 2022–2023 bills with solar export data but lack itemized NEM credit amounts, preventing verification of whether credits were properly reconciled during correction.

Status: Cannot Verify

Recommendation

Request original 2022–2023 bill statements to audit the correction impact on solar credits before finalizing historical analysis.

Impact on Current Analysis
